_source.displaydescription: Kirtipur, an old Newar settlement of the Kathmandu Valley is believed to be founded by King Sadāśivadeva (ca. 1099-1126 CE). The citizens of this ancient Newar city have engaged in preserving the rich tangible and intangible heritage sites that have been included in the ‘World Heritage List Nominations’ by UNESCO. The city, with its numerous temples, stūpas, caityas or arcaded platforms, dynamised by several impressive processions, festivals and other cultural activities, is a remarkable repository of cultural heritage from Nepal.  Kirtipur hosts the unique Bāghabhairava temple, Cilincva Caitya and Umāmaheśvara temple.

_source.displaydescription: The Bhurtī temple complex is located 3 km north of Nārāyaṇa, the Dailekh district headquarter. It currently comprises 22 standing śikhara temples (or devala) and one stone fountain. Architectural activity at the site can be situated between the 13th and 15th century, a time period corresponding to the latter part of the Khaśa Malla empire and the early phase of the Rāskoṭi dynasty. In 2008, the “Bhurti Temple Complex of Dailekh” was enlisted on UNESCO’s World Heritage Tentative List by the Government of Nepal (criteria ii and iv).

_source.displaydescription:
Basaḥ Hiti is one of three hitis located next to each other at the base of the Imūdvã hillock in Lalitpur. The neighborhood is mainly inhabited by the members of Poḍe caste who . Therefore, the hiti is commonly used by them.

The term vāsaḥ means medicine in the Newari language, and thus, it is believed that water from this hiti contains medicinal properties. It is said that the Rāṇā rulers used to drink water from the Vāṣah Hiti (Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City 2007, 42). The hiti has two water spouts. A statue of Bhagīratha is installed underneath the main spout (LAL0994-001) and a statue of Umāmaheśvara is placed above it.

The date of construction of the hiti is not recorded but it is assumed that it was built during the reign of Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera Rāṇā [r. 1932-1945] (Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City 2007, 39).

A certain Jayarāja Śreṣṭha renovated the hiti  in 1999 CE (VS 2056) and in 2011 CE (VS 2068) local residents, with the financial support from the Lalitpur Sub-metropolitan City, built a water storage and distribution system for the benefit of the local community. This system is still functioning.

A minor renovation of the hiti took place in 2017 CE (VS 2074) when the hitis and phalcās  in the Ālko quarter were repaired with funds from the World Bank and the Lalitpur Municipality. Unfortunately, little attention was paid to the use of authentic materials for the renovation. Due to rapid urbanization resulting in groundwater depletion, the flow of water in the hiti considerably decreases during the dry season. The local community cleans and worships the hiti on the day of the Sithinakhaḥ, the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha.

_source.displaydescription:
Hona Bāhāḥ, also known as Hoḍola Vihārā or Kṛṣṇavīra Vihāra, is a one-storey god house located southeast of the Cyasal Square. This independent bāhāḥ was established by Kṛṣṇavīra Prajāpati (Tuisiṃ Āḥju) and is sometimes also referred to as a nani. The front facade resembles a three-bayed phalcā and the sanctum is located behind the central bay. The main statues in the sanctum are Akṣobhya, Tārā and Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara. The original Akṣobhya was stolen and replaced with a new one. The northern wall of the sanctum is furnished with latticed woodwork. Above the carved entrance door is a wooden toraṇa with Akṣobhya at the centre, Prajñāpāramitā to the left and Lokeśvara to the right. Statues of Gaṇeśa, Mahākāla are attached to the front facade and a statue of Mañjuvajra resides in a niche on the west interior wall. The roof is covered with traditional tiles.

Hona Bāhāḥ is nestled between residential buildings on the west and east, two doors lead to a small courtyard to its south and the main facade faces an rectangular courtyard with a row of residential buildings. A small pañcāvali caitya was established in front of the main sanctum in 1895 CE (NS 1015). There are no records when the bāhāḥ was built, however, it is likely that it was established at the same time as the caitya. Hona Bāhāḥ was reconstructed with different bricks and types of mortar: the sanctum was rebuilt in dacīapā using cement mortar while the other walls consist of māapā, dacīapā and desiapā in mud mortar.

Kuladeva Bāhāḥ is a branch of Rudravarṇa Mahāvihāra, Oku Bāhāḥ (LAL2260). Unlike many other bāhāḥs or their branches, this Bāhāḥ has no proper kvāḥpāḥchẽ (house for the Bāhāḥ’s kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ ‘primary deity’). Instead, a small temple (kvāḥpāḥdegaḥ) made of bricks and plastered in cement, houses a brass statue of Akṣobhya as the Bāhāḥ’s kvāḥpādyaḥ inside its sanctum. The temple has a caitya shaped pinnacle, and its main entrance to the sanctum is protected with iron bars. It is capped by a toraṇa and is flanked by a Gaṇeśa (left) and a Mahākāla (right) statue.

The current brass made Akṣobhya statue is enshrined recently[1] after the previous one made of stone was stolen from the sanctum in 2012 CE (VS 2069). Two brothers, Kuladeva and Caityarāja (supported by Kuladeva’s son Mānadeva), had jointly built this Bāhāḥ, installed the aforementioned stone statue of Akṣobhya in the sanctum, and established a Dharmadhātu Manḍala in the Bāhāḥ’s courtyard in 1928 CE (NS 1048). The Caitya, which has also been erected in the courtyard, is probably older than the Bāhāḥ itself. The bell offered to the Caitya in 1920 CE (NS 1040) by the same two brothers has evidential value for dating.  Until recently, the sons of Kuladeva and Caityarāja used to perform the daily rituals in this Bāhāḥ.  They have also stopped performing its anniversary rituals which used to take place on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha (the Akṣayatṛtīyā day).

_source.displaydescription:
This Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya is located at the south-west corner of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001).

Shields above the Caitya's harmikā symbolise the four Tathāgatas: the jewel, lotus, viśvavajra and vajra. Below the dome, one can find statues of the four Tathāgatas: Vairocana (east), Mañjuśrī (north), Vajrasattva (west) and Amitābha (south). In addition to this, four Tārās have been placed at the corners above three layers of lotus petals. The composite of dome and drum contains eight niches and rests in turn on the pericarp of a fully opened lotus flower with three circles of petals. The Four Buddhas have been placed on a throne atop some upward-opening single-layered lotus blossoms. Statues of Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha and Amoghasiddhi have been placed on the eastern, southern, western and northern sides of the Caitya respectively. Akṣobhya’s seat is decorated with images of two elephants and Maitreya. Similarly, the southern side is decorated with images of two horses and Vajrapāṇi, the western side displays peacocks and Padmapāṇi, and the northern side exhibits images of Garuḍas and Mañjuśrī. The lower lotus is decorated with a circle of water motifs and rests upon still another socle. This socle takes a vimśatikoṇa shape and is decorated with vajra symbols. Below this, one can see a lion throne with four sculpted images lions at each of its four corners, as well as images of Caturmahārājas at each of the cardinal directions. Below the throne, one can see a vedikā and a plinth.

This Caitya was commissioned by Harṣamuni Śākya in 1958. The anniversary ritual worship of the Caitya is performed on the full moon day of Vaiśākha.
